title: Would you use one database for everything, or different databases for different parts?
summary: Splitting storage by workload only pays off where the access pattern genuinely differs. Learn to justify each specialized store against the operational cost it adds.

slides.markdown:
This question probes the simplicity-vs-fit trade-off directly. One database for everything is operationally simple — one thing to back up, monitor, and understand — but forces every workload through a storage model that fits some of them poorly.

Multiple specialized stores fit each workload better but multiply what your team has to operate. A strong answer splits storage **only** where the access pattern is genuinely different, and justifies each addition against the operational cost it adds — not by defaulting to one database, or reaching for a new one per feature.

Ask: **which parts of this system have genuinely different access patterns** — full-text search, graph traversal over relationships, time-ordered writes, standard transactional lookups? Not "which parts could theoretically use a different database," but which parts are actively fighting the current one.

Also ask how big the team is and what its operational maturity looks like — a two-person team maintaining five specialized databases is a different risk profile than a platform team with dedicated ops for each.

Structure it as: **split storage only where the access pattern is genuinely different, and justify each addition against its ops cost individually.** Don't propose a store-per-feature list; propose one default store and name the specific exceptions that earn their own system.

"I'd keep accounts and orders relational by default. I'd add a search index only because full-text search over posts is a fundamentally different access pattern a relational LIKE query can't serve well at this scale." Each addition is argued for, not assumed.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a social app's three-store split
slides.markdown:
![App tier backed by a relational DB, a graph DB, and a search index, each for a distinct access pattern](assets/polyglot-persistence.svg)

Each store here exists because the relational default genuinely can't serve one specific access pattern well: multi-hop "friends of friends" traversal for the graph store, and full-text relevance ranking for the search index.

Accounts and sessions stay relational because nothing about their access pattern demands otherwise — the split is deliberate, not automatic.

assets.alt: App tier backed by a relational DB, a graph DB, and a search index, each for a distinct access pattern

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: forcing the follow graph into the relational store
slides.markdown:
To see why a graph store earns its place, look at what happens without it. "Friends of friends who also follow this page" as a relational query means multiple self-joins on a follows table, each join multiplying the row count, with performance degrading sharply as the traversal depth grows past two or three hops.

A graph database represents this natively — a traversal query walks edges directly rather than joining a table against itself repeatedly — turning an increasingly expensive query into one that stays fast regardless of how deep the traversal goes.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the operational runbook difference
slides.markdown:
Backing up one relational instance means one backup schedule, one restore procedure, one set of alerts, one on-call runbook to learn. Backing up three different storage systems means three of each — a graph database's backup format and restore procedure are nothing like a relational dump-and-restore, and a search index's snapshot mechanism is different again.

This is the concrete shape of "operational cost": not an abstract complexity tax, but a literal multiplication of runbooks, monitoring dashboards, and on-call knowledge the team has to maintain and keep current.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Say this explicitly: **each specialized store fits its workload better, but adds an operational surface — backups, monitoring, upgrades, on-call knowledge — that now multiplies with every store added.** You're not getting a better fit for free.

A candidate who names this cost, and still argues for the split because the fit genuinely justifies it, sounds more senior than one who either defaults to one database reflexively or proposes a specialized store for every feature without weighing what it costs to run.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: three databases means three things to operate
slides.markdown:
Justify it with the specific query each store makes possible that the relational default can't serve at acceptable latency or complexity — not with a vague "it's the right tool for the job." For the follow graph, name the actual query (multi-hop traversal) and the actual relational alternative (repeated self-joins degrading with depth) you're avoiding.

Frame the ask to your team as a cost-benefit: the added on-call surface against a concrete, currently-painful query that would otherwise stay slow or unbuildable. A vague appeal to "best practice" doesn't survive this follow-up.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: keeping the search index in sync with the relational store
slides.markdown:
Since there's no cross-database transaction, syncing has to be explicit: on a post edit, write to the relational store first (source of truth), then publish an event or trigger a job that updates the search index. Most designs accept the index being eventually consistent — a few seconds stale after an edit — rather than trying to make it synchronous.

Name the failure mode too: if the sync step fails, the index silently drifts from the source of truth. A common mitigation is a periodic reconciliation job that re-syncs any documents that haven't been touched recently, catching drift that a single missed event would otherwise leave permanently stale.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a specialized database per feature, unweighed
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This feature would work well with a graph database, so let's add one" — repeated for every feature that has some plausible specialized fit.

**Why it's wrong:** each addition compounds the operational surface the team maintains, and "would work well with" is a much lower bar than "genuinely can't be served adequately by what we already run." A team can end up operating five databases where two would have sufficed.

**Correct model:** default to one store, and add a specialized one only when the access pattern is genuinely a poor fit for the default — argued with a specific query, not a general affinity.

"I'd default to one database and only add a specialized store where the access pattern genuinely doesn't fit — a graph store for deep relationship traversal, a search index for full-text ranking, both things a relational store handles poorly at scale. Each addition costs real operational surface: its own backup, monitoring, and on-call knowledge, multiplying with every store I add. So I'd argue for each one with the specific query it unlocks, not a general sense that it 'fits the domain,' and keep everything else on the simplest default that works."

The general version of this trade-off, beyond any one interview scenario, lives in [polyglot persistence](polyglot-persistence).
